Name: Athens (Acropolis) (אתונה (יוון))
Description: A cave leading to an underground corridor with a spring at its base, accessed by eight flights of stairs from the Acropolis. The entrance was sealed during sieges. Pottery dates the end of its use to the second half of the 13th century BCE.

Name: Mezer (מצר)
Description: A deep water shaft, 52m deep, with a staircase descending along its side, dug to reach groundwater. The excavation was documented in two texts and took 100 days with 120 workers. The bottom was moist, suggesting groundwater was reached.

Name: Mycenae (מיקנה (יוון))
Description: An underground system with hidden clay pipes transporting water from the Perseia spring (360m away) to an internal reservoir within the city walls, accessed by a stepped passage. Dated to the 13th century BCE. Additionally, two wells were found within the city walls, and two external springs served settlements outside the walls.

Name: Tel Ashdod (תל אשדוד)
Description: A plastered pool (4162) measuring 3.2x1.5m, found in Area G within a governor's house or palace (Strata XIV-XVII, Late Bronze Age II). It had two phases, with a brick layer beneath the plaster floor, and a drainage channel leading to a stone-lined drainage pit. Water likely collected from roofs or was manually brought from a well.

Name: Tel Beit Shemesh (תל בית שמש)
Description: Numerous rock-cut, plastered cisterns (at least 24) were found, dating to Stratum IV (Late Bronze Age). They had narrow necks built up with fieldstones and a sump at the bottom. The widespread use of plaster is highlighted.

Name: Tel Beth Shean (תל בית שאן)
Description: A deep well, 13m deep and 0.86m in diameter, found in the southeastern part of Tel Beit She'an. Its walls were built of bricks for 11.9m, with the rest being earlier fill. Dated to Stratum IXa (14th century BCE).

Name: Tel Gamma (תל ג'מה)
Description: A sealed well, evidenced by large stones with rope marks and a depression that fills with water, located 400m southwest of Nahal Besor, at the foot of the acropolis. Possibly dates to the initial phase of the lower city in the Late Bronze Age.

Name: Tel Hazor (תל חצור)
Description: A large underground water reservoir (No. 357) in the Upper City, within the Late Bronze Age palace area (Stratum XIV). It features a built entrance corridor with a corbelled arch and a rock-cut section extending 30m to a depth of 8.5m, ending in a cruciform shape. It was plastered and had carved steps, with a capacity of about 150 cubic meters. Initially, it might have been a burial cave (Stratum XV) before being converted to a reservoir. A bottle-shaped cistern, dated to the Late Bronze Age, found in the western part of the Iron Age water system entrance. Its neck was destroyed during the Iron Age construction, but it contained many intact Late Bronze Age vessels.

Name: Tel Taanach (תל תענך)
Description: A square shaft (1.45m side, 7.4m preserved height) initially intended as a stepped well to groundwater, but excavation was halted. The entire system, including the shaft, was plastered to serve as a reservoir. Dated to Late Bronze Age I, possibly after Thutmose III's campaign (1468 BCE).

Name: Tiryns (טירינס (יוון))
Description: Two steep underground passages (30m long, 10m within walls) led through the 10m thick walls to two subterranean cisterns fed by springs. The passages, covered by corbelled arches, ended in small basins where water seeped from rock fissures.
